Will local candidate quality, incumbency, and district-level dynamics materially favor Fidesz in marginal constituencies in 2026?
A) Yes. Fidesz’s local organization, incumbency, and candidate advantages will be strong enough to secure many close district contests.
B) No. District-level dynamics will be competitive enough that Fidesz cannot rely on broad marginal-seat advantages.

Will a major external or domestic shock shortly before the election produce a rally-around-incumbent effect or otherwise sharply reshape voting behavior?
A) No. No major late shock meaningfully boosts the incumbent bloc; the campaign remains on expected fundamentals.
B) Yes. A war, migration crisis, EU conflict, opposition scandal, or other shock produces a strong incumbent rally or otherwise sharply shifts votes toward the leading bloc.

Will the leading pro-government party or coalition retain enough popular support by 2026 to be competitive for a two-thirds seat share rather than merely a plurality or narrow majority?
A) Yes. The leading governing force remains sufficiently popular nationwide and locally that a supermajority is electorally plausible.
B) No. The governing force’s underlying support erodes enough that a two-thirds seat outcome becomes very difficult even if it remains the largest bloc.

Will the main anti-Fidesz opposition forces coordinate effectively in single-member districts in a way that substantially reduces vote-splitting against the strongest pro-government candidate?
A) Yes. Opposition forces avoid destructive district-by-district competition and rally behind common candidates in enough constituencies to constrain the governing bloc’s seat bonus.
B) No. Opposition parties largely fail to coordinate in single-member districts, allowing repeated anti-government vote-splitting that benefits the leading government candidate.

Will at least one opposition challenger or alliance become credible enough nationally by 2026 to consolidate tactical voting against the dominant governing force in many competitive districts?
A) No opposition challenger or alliance will become sufficiently credible to unify anti-incumbent tactical voting across a large number of districts.
B) At least one opposition challenger or alliance will become credible enough to consolidate anti-incumbent tactical voting in many districts and block a supermajority.

Will economic and social conditions before the election be good enough for the incumbent bloc to avoid a broad anti-incumbent swing large enough to block a supermajority?
A) Yes. Conditions will not deteriorate enough to produce a large anti-incumbent wave; the government side will remain electorally resilient.
B) No. Economic or social conditions will worsen enough to create a substantial anti-incumbent swing that blocks any supermajority path for the government side.

Will political and economic conditions before the election produce a strong enough anti-incumbent swing to substantially reduce the leading party’s path to two-thirds of seats?
A) Political and economic conditions will not produce a strong enough anti-incumbent swing to seriously endanger the leading party’s path to a supermajority.
B) Political and economic conditions will produce a strong anti-incumbent swing that materially weakens the leading party’s path to a supermajority.

Will Fidesz-KDNP retain a clear national vote advantage by election time, rather than facing a near-tie or trailing a unified challenger?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will still hold a meaningful national lead by 2026.
B) No. Fidesz-KDNP will face a near-even race or fall behind nationally by 2026.

Will scandals, elite splits, or defections within the incumbent camp remain limited enough that the governing coalition contests the election from a position of unity?
A) Yes. The incumbent camp will remain united, with no major split that meaningfully reduces its seat-winning efficiency.
B) No. Significant scandals, factional conflict, or defections will weaken the incumbent coalition’s electoral efficiency.

Will the emergence or persistence of significant third-party competitors siphon enough votes from either the opposition bloc or Fidesz to prevent any one party or coalition from reaching two-thirds?
A) No. Third-party leakage will stay limited, or will be absorbed into a larger coalition framework, so it will not seriously block a two-thirds outcome.
B) Yes. Meaningful third-party competition will fragment the vote enough to deny either major camp the seat concentration needed for a supermajority.

Will Fidesz-KDNP remain the dominant unified governing alliance entering the 2026 election, rather than suffering a major split that fragments its vote and candidacies?
A) Yes. Fidesz-KDNP will remain organizationally cohesive and contest the election as a unified dominant alliance.
B) No. The governing alliance will face a major split, defection, or coordination failure that significantly fragments its electoral strength.

Will institutional or legal changes before the election further advantage the incumbent bloc in converting votes into seats?
A) Yes. Additional rule or administrative changes increase incumbent seat-conversion efficiency.
B) No. No further meaningful legal or institutional advantage is introduced beyond the status quo.

Will any plausible post-election coalition other than a single dominant party be cohesive and large enough to cross the two-thirds seat threshold?
A) No non-dominant-party coalition will be both cohesive and large enough to reach two-thirds of seats.
B) A non-dominant-party coalition could be cohesive and large enough to reach two-thirds of seats.

Will the anti-incumbent opposition coordinate effectively enough that most single-member districts become genuine one-on-one contests rather than fragmented multi-cornered races?
A) Yes. Opposition parties will cooperate in most constituencies, limiting vote-splitting and making district races far more competitive.
B) No. Opposition coordination will remain incomplete or break down, leaving many districts divided among multiple anti-incumbent candidates.

Will Hungary’s electoral system and district structure still provide a large enough winner’s bonus in 2026 that a strong but not overwhelming Fidesz lead could translate into a supermajority of seats?
A) The electoral system and district structure will still generate a strong winner’s bonus capable of producing a supermajority.
B) The electoral system and district structure will not generate a winner’s bonus large enough to produce a supermajority absent overwhelming support.

Will anti-incumbent pressures by 2026—economic dissatisfaction, scandal, voter fatigue, or elite defections—be strong enough to substantially reduce Fidesz’s vote and district performance?
A) No. Economic or political wear-and-tear will not be severe enough to fundamentally dent Fidesz’s dominance.
B) Yes. By 2026 cumulative dissatisfaction, economic strain, or scandals will significantly weaken Fidesz’s electoral position.

Will the electoral alliance structure on the opposition side remain sufficiently fragmented that the leading governing bloc can win many single-member districts with pluralities rather than majorities?
A) Yes. Opposition fragmentation persists enough that the incumbent bloc captures many single-member districts on divided opposition votes.
B) No. The opposition is sufficiently coordinated that most competitive districts become one-on-one contests.

Will the electoral system and district map generate a large seat bonus for the vote-leading party or coalition?
A) The electoral system and district boundaries will translate a modest-to-strong vote plurality into a disproportionately large parliamentary seat share, potentially reaching two-thirds.
B) The electoral system will still give some winner’s bonus, but not enough to turn the likely vote margin into a two-thirds supermajority.

Will the opposition enter the election in a sufficiently unified and disciplined electoral arrangement to avoid major anti-Fidesz vote-splitting in single-member districts?
A) Yes. Opposition actors will coordinate effectively enough—whether through a joint list, disciplined district allocations, or de facto tactical voting—to minimize wasted anti-incumbent votes.
B) No. Opposition parties will remain too fragmented, mistrustful, or strategically misaligned, leading to enough vote-splitting or coordination failure to block a supermajority path.

Will anti-Fidesz forces coordinate effectively enough in single-member districts to avoid splitting the vote against Fidesz in a large share of competitive constituencies?
A) Opposition parties and movements will fail to sustain disciplined one-on-one coordination in enough districts, leaving many anti-government votes fragmented.
B) Opposition actors will manage significantly better tactical coordination, producing many more direct incumbent-versus-challenger races in the districts that matter.

Will opposition parties that fail to coordinate or clear list thresholds waste enough votes to materially increase the leading party’s seat share?
A) Yes. A meaningful share of opposition or minor-party votes will be wasted through fragmentation or failure to cross thresholds.
B) No. Most relevant opposition votes will be efficiently consolidated, and few votes will be wasted below thresholds.

If no single party wins two-thirds alone, will post-election coalition bargaining plausibly combine enough seats under a stable governing arrangement to cross the supermajority threshold?
A) Yes. Post-election bargaining could create a coalition that surpasses the supermajority threshold even if no party gets there alone.
B) No. Post-election coalition combinations capable of reaching two-thirds are politically implausible or numerically out of reach.

Will the electoral system’s district-level mechanics convert a modest vote lead into a disproportionately large seat bonus?
A) The electoral system is likely to magnify the leading bloc’s vote share into a very large seat share, especially through single-member district wins and list compensation.
B) The electoral system will not produce an outsized seat bonus this time because district races will be more competitive and compensation effects will be smaller.

Will media reach, campaign-resource asymmetry, and institutional advantage continue to give the incumbent bloc a large enough edge to preserve supermajority odds?
A) Yes. Resource, media, and institutional asymmetries remain strong enough to materially boost incumbent performance beyond raw popularity.
B) No. The incumbent’s informational and institutional advantages weaken, so campaign conditions become more competitive than expected.

If a non-Fidesz alliance or dominant opposition party emerges, will it be capable of sustaining disciplined pre-election coordination and post-election coalition cohesion sufficient to count as a supermajority-winning bloc?
A) Yes. A challenger bloc can maintain enough unity, candidate discipline, and coalition coherence to contest and then hold a supermajority as one effective electoral actor.
B) No. Even if a challenger gains momentum, coordination failures or post-election fragmentation will prevent it from functioning as a durable supermajority-winning coalition.
